title_screening: Disease Burden and Trends of Bladder Cancer in the World and BRICS from 1990 to 2021 and its Projection Until 2036: Analysis Based on the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021
abstract: Background: The continuously growing burden of bladder cancer (BCa) requires comprehensive and in-depth research to understand its dynamics and forecast its trends. Using the data from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2021 study, the current work evaluates and forecasts the trend of bladder cancer's disease burden worldwide and in BRICS countries to provide a scientific basis for the further development of targeted bladder cancer prevention and control measures Methods: This study used data from the GBD) 2021 study. Trends in new incidence, mortality, prevalence, and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) and various risk factors were assessed, and the relationship between sociodemographic indices (SDIs) and disease burden was determined. The estimated annual percentage change (EAPC) and average annual percentage change of age-standardized rates and their 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were analyzed with R 4.4.1 software and join point software to examine the trends in the disease burden of bladder cancer worldwide and in BRICS countries between 1990 and 2021. A Bayesian age-period-cohort model was also used to project the global and BRIC countries' bladder cancer disease burden from 2022 to 2036. The global disease burden of bladder cancer in 2021 featured an increase in incidence, mortality, prevalence and number of DALYs compared with that 1990. However, the EAPC of global bladder cancer between 1990 and 2021 for ASIR [EAPC=-0.36 (95%CI -0.41 to -0.3)], ASMR [EAPC=-0.98% (95%CI -1.03 to -0.94)], and ASDR [EAPC=-1.19% (95%CI -1.24 to -1.13)] showed a decreasing trend, and the change in ASPR [EAPC of 0.1% (95%CI 0.01 to 0.19)] was relatively stable. Among the BRICS countries, South Africa had the highest burden of bladder cancer in 1990-2021, and its burden increased most significantly in 1994-1997. By contrast, Egypt had the lowest burden, with the most significant decrease observed in 2001-2005. The disease burden of bladder cancer was positively correlated with the SDI worldwide and in BRICS countries. In terms of risk factors, smoking was the leading attributable cause of ASDR and ASMR in 2021, followed by high fasting plasma glucose worldwide and in BRICS countries. Projections indicated that the global disease burden will show a decreasing trend from 2022 to 2036, but some of the BRICS countries will continue to experience an increasing disease burden. Interpretation(s): The disease burden of bladder cancer has improved in recent years but remains a major public health challenge worldwide and in BRICS countries. Hence, investment in primary health care must be further increased, the innovation and application of medical technology must be promoted, targeted and comprehensive bladder cancer health education programs must be developed, healthy lifestyle interventions must be implemented, and cooperation and exchanges on bladder cancer prevention and treatment must be actively developed among countries. title_screening: Global, Regional, and National Burden and Quality of Care for Type 1 Diabetes in the Elderly (65+) from 1990 to 2021: A Secondary Analysis of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021
abstract:
Background: Analyze the trends in disease burden and quality of care for type 1 diabetes among individuals aged 65 and older from 1990 to 2021, and explore the potential for improvement.
Research design and methods: Utilizing data from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021, we assessed disease burden and used the Quality of Care Index (QCI) to quantify care standards. We analyzed variations in QCI by age, gender, geography, and Sociodemographic Index (SDI), using frontier analysis to identify potential improvements.
Findings: From 1990 to 2021, incidence and prevalence rates of type 1 diabetes in the elderly increased, while mortality and DALYs decreased. The global QCI rose from 87.81 to 94.88, indicating an 11.04% improvement. Females saw more significant care advancements, with reduced gender disparities (Gender Disparity Ratio dropped from 1.03 to 1.01). High SDI regions showed superior care quality despite a larger burden. QCI positively correlated with SDI, highlighting better care in higher SDI regions but challenges in low-middle and low SDI areas. Middle-high SDI countries were identified as having significant potential for care enhancement.
Interpretation: The global burden of type 1 diabetes in the elderly has decreased, with improved care quality, yet disparities remain across age, gender, and SDI. Women received slightly better care; regions with lower SDI face difficulties. Middle-high SDI countries hold considerable potential for further improvement. Targeted policies should focus on these regions, addressing gender-specific needs to ensure balanced diabetes management in the aging population.

title_screening: Expanding the Health Workforce in Mozambique to Achieve the Sustainable Development Goal for Under-5 Mortality: A Spatial Microsimulation Analysis Through 2030
abstract:
Background: Health workforce (HWF) density is a key determinant of under-5 mortality rates (U5MR) in Sub-Saharan Africa. We estimated the impact of alternative HWF expansion policies on U5MR in Mozambique from 2022 to 2030.
Methods: We created an individual-level spatial microsimulation model using a representative cohort of children under-5, estimating the effects of various HWF density scenarios on U5MR with a multivariable logistic function. The model included provincial fixed effects, secular trends, individual demographic and socioeconomic changes, and health-related characteristics.
Findings: In comparison to a business-as-usual scenario (BAU), increasing HWF densities, so to achieve the U5MR SDG goal, could result in substantially lower U5MR (Rate Ratio (RR): 0.63, 95% Uncertainty Intervals (95%UI): 0.49-0.81) and 103,401 (95%UI: 74,781-130,525) avoided child deaths up to 2030. If, instead of the BAU scenario, we compare it to a resource-scarce scenario in which the HWF density evolution stagnates until 2030, the difference increases (RR: 0.52, 95%UI: 0.41-0.66) and the total number of avoided child deaths would amount to 150,659 (UI95%:123,417-178,316). A HWF scenario with a more equitable distribution of healthcare workers, prioritizing areas with higher U5MR while maintaining the same HWF density as the BAU scenario, would result in a reduced U5MR and a 2030 provincial U5MR Disparity Index of 33, compared to 38 in the BAU scenario.
Interpretation: Increasing HWF density could significantly reduce child mortality and prevent a substantial number of child deaths over the next decade in Sub-Saharan Africa, greatly contributing to the potential achievement of SDG 3.2 by 2030. title_screening: Global, Regional, and National Prevalence of Inguinal, Femoral, and Abdominal Hernias from 1990 to 2021: Age-Period-Cohort Analysis with Future Burden Prediction
abstract: Background: Hernias remain a significant global health issue. It is estimated that approximately 20 million inguinal hernia repairs are performed annually worldwide. This figure is expected to increase as the global population continues to grow and age. Consequently, we utilized the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) database to analyze the current status of the global hernia burden and to project trends in this burden through 2035. Method(s): We analyzed the GBD 2021 database to assess the burden of inguinal, femoral, and ventral hernias across 204 countries and territories worldwide from 1990 to 2021. We collected data on incidence, mortality, age-standardized incidence rates (ASIR), and age-standardized mortality rates (ASMR). Additionally, we examined the effects of age, period, and cohort on the trends in hernia incidence and mortality using an age-period-cohort (APC) model. A total of 20 age cohorts were established using 5-year intervals for both age and time periods. Furthermore, we employed connected-point regression analysis to identify key years associated with changes in the age-standardized rates (ASR) of total hernias. Taking into account current and future demographic changes, we utilized Bayesian age-period cohort (BAPC) modeling to predict hernia incidence, the corresponding number of deaths, and ASR through 2035. Result(s): This study demonstrated that from 1990 to 2021, the global incidence of hernia cases increased by 25.49%, reaching a total of 7.24 million cases, while the corresponding ASR decreased by 16%. Additionally, the global mortality rate associated with hernias rose by 13.99%, despite a 45.16% reduction in the ASMR. Between 1990 and 2021, significant downward trends in both the ASIR and ASMR were observed across most Socio-Demographic Index (SDI) regions. The prognosis for hernias is more favorable in populations residing in areas with high SDI. Furthermore, the global prevalence of hernias is significantly higher in men than in women, with both morbidity and mortality progressively increasing with age. Older adults, particularly men aged 60 to 70 years, exhibit a higher incidence of hernias, while the highest mortality rates are observed in individuals around the age of 80 years. Projections from 1990 to 2035 indicate that by 2035, global hernia morbidity and mortality will continue to rise, while ASIR and ASMR are expected to decline. Conclusion(s): The results of this study indicate that global morbidity and mortality associated with inguinal, femoral, and ventral hernias continue to rise. The burden of these conditions varies across different regions and countries. Incidence and mortality rates for hernias remain higher among older adults and men. In conclusion, inguinal, femoral, and ventral hernias represent a significant public health challenge that must not be overlooked. Therefore, healthcare strategies aimed at reducing the incidence of inguinal, femoral, and abdominal hernias should be further developed and implemented. title_screening: Global Burden, Temporal Trends, and Risk Factors for Burkitt Lymphoma from 1990 to 2021 with Predictions to 2040: A Systematic Analysis for the 2021 Global Burden of Disease Study
abstract: Background: Burkitt lymphoma (BL) exhibits distinct epidemiological patterns and possesses complex risk factors. This study aims to assess the global burden and temporal trends of BL from 1990 to 2021, and to explore the potential noninfectious risk factors associated with the incidence and mortality rates of BL. Method(s): Data on BL were extracted from the 2021 Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study to estimate its health burden in terms of four metrics: incidence, mortality, prevalence, and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). Subgroups were stratified by age, sex, geography, and socio-demographic index (SDI). The estimated annual percentage change (EAPC) was employed to quantify the temporal trends. A decomposition analysis was conducted to evaluate the factors contributing to the changes in DALYs. Health burden predictions were performed through the Bayesian age-period-cohort (BAPC) model. Noninfectious risk factors were identified and analyzed utilizing summary exposure values (SEVs) to assess their impacts on BL incidence and mortality. Finding(s): There was a growing trend in the global health burden of Burkitt lymphoma from 1990 to 2021, whereas a decreasing trend was predicted from 2021 to 2040. The health burden was markedly higher in males, in age groups under 20 years and over 54 years, and among patients in High-income regions and sub-Saharan Africa. High SDI areas, with a higher proportion of elderly patients, demonstrated an increase in health burden from 1990 to 2021; low SDI areas, with a higher proportion of pediatric patients, showed a decrease. Disease severity served as a uniformly negative factor for changes in DALYs across all GBD regions, albeit to varying degrees. Several noninfectious risk factors, such as low bone mineral density, a diet low in vegetables, and childhood sexual abuse, exhibited positive associations with increased incidence and mortality of BL among specific subgroups; tobacco use, kidney dysfunction, and iron deficiency exhibited inverse associations. Interpretation(s): Burkitt lymphoma demonstrated unique distribution patterns in age, sex, and geography. Despite the predicted decrease in the global health burden of BL from 2021 to 2040, there remained an urgent need for the development and implementation of tailored preventive measures and improved management strategies. Further investigations into the heterogeneity in risk factors for BL are essential for informing the development of more effective health policies and clinical practices. title_screening: Trends, Inequality, and Future Projections of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy: A Global Analysis from 1992 to 2021
abstract: Background: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy (HDP) poses a serious risk to maternal health and has implications for fetal development and long-term health. Methods: We obtained data from the Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD) 2021 regarding the incidence, mortality, and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) among women of childbearing age (WCBA) aged 15-49 years across 204 countries and territories from 1992 to 2021. Analyses encompassed the slope index of inequality and concentration index for measuring health disparities, decomposition analysis to ascertain determinants of disease burden variations, Joinpoint regression analysis for evaluating temporal trends, and the Bayesian age-period-cohort (BAPC) model for forecasting future disease burden trends. Results: The global incidence of HDP, deaths and cases of DALYs in WCBA in 2021 were 17997261.34, 37578.85 and 2438170.19 respectively. The incidence of HDP, mortality and DALYs have declined over the last 30 years. The AAPC for incidence, mortality and DALYs were -0.5 (95% UI: -0.52 to -0.48), -2.1 (95% UI: -2.14 to -2.07) and -2.04 (95% UI: -2.07 to -2.01), respectively. The observed inequality has decreased, as evidenced by the reduction in the disparity of DALYs between countries with the highest and lowest SDI, which declined from 928 years in 1992 to 325 years in 2021. It is noteworthy that despite the decline in projected HDP of pregnancy incidence, mortality and DALYs, current inequalities remain substantial. Conclusion: The global burden of HDP has diminished; however, notable disparities remain, particularly in regions with low SDI. Refined policies and preventive measures are necessary to effectively address HDP among WCBA. title_screening: Global, Regional, and National Burden and Trends of Eye Cancer, 1990-2021: A Systematic Analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021
abstract: Background: Eye cancer, an uncommon eye cancer, contributes to 0.1% of global cancer-related fatalities and poses a threat to lives. The infrequency of eye cancer instances has resulted in insufficient research into its epidemiological patterns. The research makes use of every piece of data and the Global Burden of Disease, Injury, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) to analyse current data on eye cancer's impact and patterns at various levels - global, regional, and national - essential for informed health care, prevention, and resource distribution strategies. Methods: Utilizing the GBD database, this research calculated the incidence, prevalence, mortality, and disability-adjusted life year (DALY) figures, along with age-standardized annual rates per 100,000 individuals for total eye cancer across 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2021. It offered point estimates accompanied by 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs). The assessment focused on the evolving patterns in eye cancer prevalence, utilising both the average annual percentage change (AAPC) and the percentage change. Findings: In 2021, the global incidence, prevalence, death, and DALYs cases of eye cancer were 0.03 million (95% uncertainty interval [UI] 0.03-0.04), 0.28 million (95% UI 0.22-0.33), 0.01 million (95% UI 0.00-0.01) and 0.47 million (95% UI 0.35-0.57). We observed geographical differences in age-standardised eye cancer incidence, prevalence, death, and DALYs, with the lowest in North Africa and the Middle East and the highest in Sub-Saharan Africa. Over the past 32 years, global incidence rates and prevalence rates globally have increased, with an AAPC of 0.21 (95% UI 0.13 to 0.29) and 0.29 (95% UI 0.14 to 0.43), while death rates and DALYs rates have decreased with an AAPC of -0.76 (95% UI -0.86 to -0.66) and -0.69 (95% UI -0.81 to -0.56). Interpretation: Globally, eye cancer, though uncommon, is a lethal condition that imposes a considerable health strain. Between 1990 and 2021, the incidence of eye cancer escalated. There is an immediate need for feasible, reachable, and cost-effective strategies to enhance the monitoring, prevention, immediate treatment, and recovery of eye cancer to lessen its impact. title_screening: Analysis of Health, Environmental, and Socioeconomic Determinants of Cholera Severity in Conflict-Affected Tigray Region, Ethiopia: Evidence from the Cholera Outbreak Report
abstract: Background: Cholera is a life-threatening diarrheal disease caused by the ingestion of food or water contaminated with V.cholerae. It remains a major public health concern, particularly in low- and middle-income countries with inadequate WaSH systems. Ethiopia, specifically the Tigray region, has experienced recurring cholera outbreaks, exacerbated by conflict, displacement, and ravaged health infrastructure. Despite efforts to control cholera, the disease still continues to affect avalanche of populations, resulting in significant morbidity and mortality, in this war-ridden region.AimThis study aims to analyze the cholera outbreak in Tigray, Ethiopia, from July 25 to October 4, 2024, examining the outbreak's spread, clinical outcomes, and key demographic, health, and environmental factors influencing cholera severity to inform future public health interventions. Method(s): A retrospective descriptive study was conducted using data from 553 confirmed cholera cases reported across 27 woredas in Mekelle, Eastern, Central, and North Western zones of Tigray. The study utilized univariate descriptive statistics, bivariate chi-square analysis, and multivariate ordinal logistic regression to assess the impact of various predictors on cholera severity. Spatial and temporal analyses, including Getis-Ord Gi* hotspot analysis, were also conducted to scrutinize high-risk areas and epidemic trends. Result(s): The analysis revealed a peak in cholera cases in early August, with 342 cases in Asgede and smaller outbreaks in other woredas. Case Fatality Rate (CFR) was highest in Tsimbla (0.18%) and Asgede (0.30%), and the overall CFR for the region was approximately 2.00%. Multivariate analysis identified significant risk factors for severe cholera, including lack of contact with suspected Acute Watery Diarrhea (AWD) patients (OR: 0.281, p < 0.001), lack of household disinfection practices (OR: 0.410, p < 0.001), and reliance on unsafe water sources. Timely treatment within two days significantly reduced the risk of severe dehydration (OR: 0.129, p < 0.001). Vaccination against cholera showed a protective effect, with 38.5% of vaccinated individuals experiencing severe dehydration compared to 79.3% of unvaccinated individuals.ConclusionThe cholera outbreak in Tigray posed a significant public health challenge, particularly among populations with limited access to clean water and sanitation facilities. The findings underscore the importance of vaccination, early treatment, and improved WaSH infrastructure in reducing cholera severity. High CFR and delayed treatment highlight the need for rapid medical intervention in future outbreaks. Key Recommendation: To mitigate future cholera outbreaks in Tigray and similar regions, public health authorities should prioritize expanding cholera vaccination coverage, improving access to clean water and sanitation, and ensuring timely healthcare interventions. Strengthening surveillance systems and increasing public awareness of cholera prevention strategies are also critical for reducing transmission and fatalities. title_screening: Reemergence of cholera in Haiti
abstract: Cholera was absent from Haiti until an inadvertent introduction by United Nations security forces in October 2010. The ensuing epidemic sickened 820,000 and caused 9,792 reported deaths<sup>1</sup>. The last cholera case in Haiti was recorded in January 2019, and in February 2022, Haiti was declared to have eliminated cholera<sup>2</sup>. In late September of 2022, a new outbreak began in Port-au-Prince and rapidly expanded to 964 suspected cases by mid-October of which 115 were confirmed by culture.<sup>3</sup> Here, we present genomic and phenotypic analysis of the Vibrio cholerae isolated from a stool sample collected on September 30th, 2022 of an index case - a 10-year-old girl who presented with watery diarrhea and severe dehydration - to address the origins of the epidemic. The 2022 V. cholerae isolate shares phenotypes with the 2010 outbreak strain. Both strains are V. cholerae serogroup O1 of the Ogawa serotype and have similar antibiograms, including resistance to trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and low-level resistance to ciprofloxacin (Supp. Table 1,2). This resistance profile is consistent among several other isolates from the current outbreak, suggesting that the strain isolated from the index case is representative of the ongoing epidemic. To decipher the relationship between the current outbreak strain and other toxigenic O1 El Tor strains from the ongoing seventh pandemic of cholera, we sequenced the 9/30/2022 isolate, along with four 2021-2022 isolates from Dhaka, Bangladesh (Supp. Table 2). Phylogenetic analyses of over 1,200 isolates revealed that the 2022 Haiti index case clusters extremely closely with isolates from the 2010 outbreak in Haiti (Figure 1). This isolate is similarly closely related to 2010 Nepal isolates that were the origin of the initial outbreak as well as to 2013 strains from Mexico that were thought to have spread from Haiti<sup>4</sup> and is divergent from currently circulating Bangladesh isolates. Haiti 2022 and Haiti 2010 isolates have identical ctxB (ctxB7) and other virulence factors (Supp. Table 3) and produce similar quantities of cholera toxin (Supp. Figure 1). These analyses strongly suggest the reemergence of cholera in Haiti is caused by a descendant of the V. cholerae strain that gave rise to the 2010 epidemic. However, no cases of cholera were confirmed between 2019 and 2022 despite ongoing surveillance. Several explanations for the recrudescence of this strain are possible. The first is that toxigenic V. cholerae O1 persisted in Haiti through sub-clinical human infection and has recurred in the setting of waning population immunity coupled with a crisis in lack of clean water and sanitation. A second non-exclusive possibility is that this V. cholerae strain has persisted in environmental reservoirs. Finally, since the Haiti outbreak was ultimately transmitted to other countries in Latin America<sup>4</sup>, a third much less likely explanation given the absence of recent cholera cases in the region is that the current strain could have been reintroduced to Haiti from a nearby country. These findings, along with the resurgence of cholera in several parts of the world<sup>5</sup> despite available tools, suggest that cholera control and prevention efforts must be redoubled. title_screening: Global, Regional, and National Time Trends in Mortality for Ischemic Heart Disease, 1990-2019: An Age-Period-Cohort Analysis for the Global Burden of Disease 2019 Study
abstract: Introduction: Ischemic heart disease (IHD) is the leading cause of mortality and disability worldwide. This study investigates the global trend in IHD mortality across 204 countries and territories over the past 30 years and explores the influence of age, period, and birth cohort. Method(s): We retrieved the IHD mortality data from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2019 study. We assessed the temporal trend in the number of deaths, all-age mortality rates, and age-standardized mortality rates across countries grouped by the Socio-Demographic Index (SDI) quintiles. We also applied an Age-Period-Cohort (APC) model to estimate overall annual percentage changes in mortality (net drifts) and annual percentage changes in specific age groups (local drifts). We further utilized the APC model to distinguish the independent effects of age, period, and birthing cohort on temporal mortality trends. Result(s): Between 1990 and 2019, global IHD deaths increased from 5.70 million (95% UI: 5.41-5.90) to 9.14 million (95% UI: 8.40-9.74). All-age mortality rates also rose significantly, with a notable shift in deaths toward older populations (>= 70 years). The global net drift in IHD mortality declined by 1.1% annually (95% CI: -1.17% to -1.04%), with high-SDI countries experiencing the greatest decline (-2.84%, 95% CI: -3.05% to -2.64%) . Aging, period, and cohort effects manifest a general declining trend. Among all countries, the Philippines showed the largest positive net drift (3.6%, 95% CI: 3.33% to 3.86%). Key global risk factors included hypertension, elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, ambient particulate matter pollution, and smoking. Notably, low temperature emerged as the leading environmental risk factor in high-SDI countries. Conclusion(s): From 1990 to 2019, the global burden and temporal trends of IHD mortality varied substantially across SDI quintiles, sexes, geographic regions, and countries. These disparities underscore the importance of region-specific, risk-differentiated, and cost-effective IHD prevention and management strategies. title_screening: Impact of Macrolide Resistance on Azithromycin for Prevention of Rehospitalization or Death Among Children Discharged from Hospitals in Western Kenya
abstract:
Background: The Toto Bora trial tested whether a 5-day course of azithromycin reduced the risk of re-hospitalization or death in the 6 months following hospitalization among Kenyan children and found no overall benefit. We hypothesized that macrolide resistance in gut microbes could modify azithromycin's effect.
Methods: From June 2016 to November 2019, Kenyan children aged 1-59 months were enrolled at hospital discharge and randomized to azithromycin or placebo. DNA from fecal samples and E. coli isolates was analyzed for common macrolide resistance genes. Cox proportional hazards regression models of time to rehospitalization or death with an interaction term between the randomization arm and each macrolide-resistance gene were used.
Results: Among 1,393 children tested, 94.7% had at least one macrolide-resistance gene in their fecal DNA at hospital discharge; most commonly mph(A) (68.6%; 955/1393), followed by msr(D) (67.3%; (937/1393), and erm(B) (60.7%; 846/1393). Mef(A) (23.7%; 330/1393) was the only macrolide-resistance gene that modified azithromycin's effect on re-hospitalization or death (interaction p-value=0.008). In children without the mef(A) gene, azithromycin reduced the hazard of rehospitalization or death by a third (HR=0.66, 95%CI: 0.45-0.99) whereas among children with the mef(A) gene, there was a higher risk in those randomized to azithromycin (HR=2.72, 95%CI: 1.21-6.09). The effect size of azithromycin's impact on mortality and rehospitalization as separate outcomes in children with and without mef(A) were consistent but underpowered.
Interpretation: Macrolide resistance in the gut microbiome may influence the efficacy of azithromycin in children discharged from the hospital.

title_screening: Global, Regional, and National Epidemiology of Thyroid Cancer in Middle-Aged and Elderly Patients from 1990 to 2021: Results from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021
abstract: Background: In recent years, changes in the incidence, mortality and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) rates of thyroid cancer (TC) have occurred globally, across various regions, and among different countries. The purpose of this study is to assess the burden of TC among middle-aged and elderly patients over the course of 30 years in 204 countries and territories. Methods: Detailed information on TC among middle-aged and elderly patients from 1990 to 2021 was collected from the Global Burden of Disease Database 2021 (GBD2021). Adopted incidence, mortality, disability-adjusted lifeyears (DALYs) and corresponding Estimated Annual Percentage Changes (EAPCs) to assess the burden of TC in middle-aged and elderly patients. In the analysis of global trends, multiple variables were carefully considered, including age, gender, and the sociodemographic Index (SDI). Furthermore, a global risk attribution analysis was conducted, and a Bayesian age-period-cohort (BAPC) model was applied to project the global burden of TC in middle-aged and elderly patients from 2021 to 2035. Results: Globally, the incidence cases of TC in middle-aged and elderly people increased by 185%, the numbers of death increased by 116%, and the DALYs increased by 108%. Over the period from 1990 to 2021, age-standardized incidence rates exhibited a global rise, whereas deaths and DALYs saw a decrease (EAPC:1.63, -0.15, -0.14, respectively). Moreover, a higher SDI is positively correlated with the ASIR. The incidence rate of TC increased in all 21 GBD regions except Central Europe. Notably, TC cases, deaths, and DALYs were consistently higher among females than males, but the gender gap is narrowing. Additionally, the highest incidences of TC in middle-aged and elderly females were in the 70-74 age group, while for males it is in the 85-89 age group. Research indicates that high BMI was a major risk factor for TC in the middle-aged and elderly population. Conclusions: The increasing incidence of TC among middle-aged and elderly adults is placing a significant burden on global healthcare systems, tailored screening and treatment strategies must be developed to account for differences across gender groups and regions. title_screening: Silent Killer Strikes During Eid-Ul-Adha: Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Outbreak in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, 2023
abstract: Background: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) poses a substantial public health threat, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, where its prevalence and epidemiological distribution remain inadequately documented. This study investigated the epidemiology, prevalence, and transmission dynamics of the 2023 CCHFV outbreak in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, during the Eid-ul-Adha season. Methods: A total of 109 suspected cases were enrolled from April to July 2023. Laboratory confirmation was performed using real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). Demographic, clinical, and epidemiological data were analyzed to identify high-risk groups and outbreak dynamics. Results: Of the suspected cases, 15 (13.76%) were confirmed CCHFV positive, with males accounting for 80% of cases (n = 12). The highest prevalence (33.33%) was recorded in Peshawar district, and 53% of cases had a history of animal exposure. A significant spike (5 cases) occurred in epidemiological week 29, following Eid-ul-Adha. Clinical symptoms included fever, body aches, confusion, and bleeding episodes, with a case fatality rate (CFR) of 26.67% (male-specific CFR: 33.33%). All female patients recovered. Conclusion: These findings highlight CCHFV as a critical public health concern in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa region. The elevated risk associated with Eid-ul-Adha, and age and gender demographics necessitates targeted awareness initiatives, preventive strategies, and strengthened surveillance during peak risk periods to mitigate transmission and future outbreaks. Study limitations include a relatively small sample size, potential selection bias, and the lack of a control group. Further research with larger sample sizes and more comprehensive data collection is needed to better understand the epidemiology and transmission dynamics of CCHFV in this region. title_screening: In-Hospital Mortality in Patients with Blunt Pelvic Trauma: A Multicenter Case-Control Study
abstract: BackgroundPelvic ring fractures occur in 3% of orthopedic trauma, with associated injuries up to 90% and mortality between 10 and 32%. There is conflicting evidence about mortality-related factors among different populations. ObjectiveTo analyze the relationship between some variables and in-hospital mortality in patients with blunt pelvic trauma.DesignA multicenter case-control study with adults admitted between 2017 and 2022 in 3 trauma centers in Medellin, Colombia.Exposures22 variables related to the patient, pre-hospital settings, trauma kinematics, medical care, and clinical course were measured.Main Outcomes and MeasuresThe main outcome was in-hospital mortality. Adjusted odds ratios were obtained.Results67 pelvic ring fracture-related deaths were identified, and 201 controls were sampled. The patient's median age was 47 years, 51,87% were men, and the prehospital transfer time had a median of 4,5 hours. Accidental events represented 96,64%. In the first 24 hours, the median lactate and base excess values were 4,55mmol/L and -6,7, respectively. Coagulopathy was detected in 32,03% of the sample. The median Injury Severity Score (ISS) was 12 points. The associated injuries were abdominal (39,55%), head (33,96%), facial (17,16%), and thoracic (15%). Severity of pelvic trauma, according to the World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) classification, was grade I at 52,99%, grade II at 18,28%, grade III at 9,33%, and grade IV at 19,4%. Pelvic preperitoneal packing (PPP) was performed in 8,58% of patients, with a median time from admission to PPP of 186 minutes. Pelvic arterial bleeding was detected in 10,81%, with a median time from admission to angioembolization of 374 minutes. Factors independently associated with in-hospital mortality were GCS[[EQUATION]]9 at the arrival (OR: 16,254, CI95%: 5,367 - 49,223) and coagulopathy in the first 72 hours (OR: 7,649, CI95%: 2,962 - 20,441). PPP was associated with reduced in-hospital mortality (OR: 0,118, CI95%: 0,036 - 0,390).ConclusionsIn patients with blunt pelvic ring injuries, a reduced state of consciousness with a GCS[[EQUATION]]9 at the arrival to the trauma bay and the development of coagulopathy in the first 72 hours were related to increased odds of mortality. Otherwise, PPP was associated with reduced odds of in-hospital mortality. Copyright © 2025, The Authors. All rights reserved.

title_screening: Systematic Analysis of the Burden of Chronic Kidney Disease Due to Type 2 Diabetes Attributable to Dietary Risks Based on the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021
abstract:
Background: Dietary factors play a crucial role in the development of chronic kidney disease due to diabetes mellitus type 2 (T2D-related CKD). However, comprehensive data on the global burden of T2D-related CKD attributable to dietary risks remain limited.
Methods: This study conducted a secondary analysis of the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study 2021. Mortality and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) of T2D-related CKD attributable to dietary risks, stratified by sex, age and sociodemographic index (SDI) quantiles, were analyzed in global, 21 regions, and 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2021.
Findings: In 2021, 79,990 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 32,730 to 128,880) death and 1,999,210 (95% CI: 856,190 to 3,167,220) DALYs of T2D-related CKD were attributable to dietary risk factors, approximately 2.5 times as many as those in 1990. The age-standardized mortality rate (ASMR) and age-standardized DALY rate (ASDR) grew with an estimated annual percentage change (EAPC) of 0.76% (95%CI: 0.69% to 0.83%) and 0.47% (95%CI: 0.41% to 0.53%). The low SDI regions experienced the highest burden of T2D-related CKD attributable to dietary risks, with ASMR of 1.16 (95% CI: 0.44 to 2.02) per 100,000 persons and the ASDR of 27.41 (95% CI: 11.32 to 46.78) per 100,000 persons. Males and the elderly over 70 years demonstrated a higher burden of T2D-related CKD influenced by dietary risks. Diet low in fruits, whole grains, and vegetables, as well as diet high in red and processed meat serve as the main dietary risks contributed to the burden of T2D-related CKD.
Interpretation: Dietary factors play a significant role in the development of T2D-related CKD. Further strategies should focus on men, the elderly, low-SDI regions and specific dietary components to mitigate dietary risks associated with T2D-related CKD.

title_screening: Global, Regional, and National Burden of Musculoskeletal Disorders, 1990-2021: An Analysis of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021 and Forecast to 2035
abstract: Background: Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) represent a primary cause of disability globally, exhibiting an escalating burden over the past three decades. This study assesses the global, regional, and national burdens of MSDs from 1990 to 2021, encompassing prevalence, incidence, disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), and mortality rates. It also projects future trends up to 2035 and explores avenues for improvement through frontier analysis. Method(s): We utilized data from the Global Burden of Disease 2021 study, analyzing MSDs across 204 countries and territories. Age-standardized rates (ASRs) for prevalence (ASPR), incidence (ASIR), DALYs (ASDR), and mortality (ASMR) were calculated. Trends were evaluated using estimated annual percentage changes (EAPC), and frontier analysis was implemented to assess the potential for reducing MSDs burdens relative to the Socio-Demographic Index (SDI). Projections to 2035 were made using the Bayesian age-period-cohort (BAPC) model. Finding(s): In 2021, there were approximately 1.686 billion prevalent cases of MSDs globally, representing a 95% increase since 1990. While the total number of cases and DALYs have risen, the ASIR and ASMR displayed declining trends, with global mortality from MSDs decreasing by 0.265% annually. Projections suggest that by 2035, the total number of MSDs cases will reach approximately 2.161 billion, with corresponding increases in DALYs and deaths. Nonetheless, ASRs are anticipated to continue their annual decline. Frontier analysis identified significant disparities between current MSDs burdens and achievable benchmarks based on developmental levels. Regions with higher SDIs exhibited substantial potential for improvement, whereas some lower-SDI regions demonstrated effective management despite limited resources. The analysis highlighted a U-shaped relationship between SDI and MSDs burden, with middle-SDI regions generally outperforming those at the low and high ends of the spectrum. Interpretation(s): The global burden of MSDs is projected to rise in absolute case numbers, underscoring the necessity for strategically targeted interventions to manage their impact effectively. Frontier analysis illuminates potential improvements, particularly in high-SDI countries, while projections indicate that enhanced access to healthcare and better resource distribution could alleviate the global MSDs burden. Addressing disparities and implementing tailored interventions are crucial for reducing MSDs-related disability and mortality. title_screening: Global, Regional, and National Burden of Road Injuries, 1990-2021, and Projections to 2050: A Systematic Analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021
abstract:
Objective: To evaluate the burden and trends in incidence, death, and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) associated with road injuries across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2021, and to forecast global and regional road injury death rates up to the year 2050.
Methods: Data were sourced from the Global Burden of Disease, Injury, and Risk Factor Study 2021 (GBD2021). The study estimated the global, regional, and national age-standardized rates (per 100,000) of incidence (ASIR), death (ASDR), and disability-adjusted life years (ASDAR) associated with road injuries, along with their 95% uncertainty intervals (95% UI). These estimates were stratified by age, sex, and socio-demographic index (SDI) for the period from 1990 to 2021.The risk factors contributing to the death and DALYs rates of road injuries and distribution as well as ranking of injury sites from road injuries were identified. The future death rates due to road injuries from 2022 to 2050 were projected by utilizing the GBD Foresight Visualization tool.
Results: While the global ranking of road injuries has decreased from the 12th leading cause of death in 1990 to the 14th in 2021,they remain the leading cause of death among individuals aged 15-24 years(ranking 1st), among 15-44 years (ranking 2nd), among 15-64 years (ranking 4th), respectively. Overall, the ASIR, ASDR, and ASDAR of road injuries in global level showed a downward trend from 1990 to 2021. But, some countries continue to exhibit a slight upward trend. At the regional level, the ASIR and SDI were positively correlated, especially when SDI were 0.30 -0.50(rho=0.58,P<0.001) and 0.62-0.75 (rho=0.46,P<0.001). In contrast, the ASDR as well as ASDAR showed a significant negative correlation with SDI. Males experienced a greater burden of road injuries compared to females. Occupational injuries are a major contributor to the DALYs burden. Meanwhile, high temperature is the only risk factor that has shown a positive EAPC of 0.12, indicating an increasing impact. Fractures of the lower extremities consistently show the highest incidence across nearly all road injury types and age groups under 70. From 2022 to 2050, global road injury death rates are projected to continue declining; yet increases are anticipated in specific high-income regions, notably Asia Pacific (e.g., Republic of Korea) and North America (e.g., The United States). Trends also vary by injury type, with projected rises in cyclist mortality in globally and several regions.
Conclusion(s): Although the ASIR, ASDR, and ASDAR of road injuries in global level showed a downward trend from 1990 to 2021,road injuries remain the leading cause of death among juveniles and young adults aged 15-44 years. Males bear a disproportionate burden, underscoring the need for targeted gender- and age-specific road safety strategies. Fractures of the lower extremities are the most common injury across all age groups under 70, pointing to the necessity of prevention programs to mitigate these injuries, which often lead to long-term disability. Additionally, high temperatures have emerged as an increasing risk factor for road injuries. Finally, the projected rise in cyclist mortality in several regions calls for enhanced safety measures, especially with the growing popularity of cycling as part of green transport initiatives.

title_screening: Global, Regional, and National Burden of Lower Extremity Peripheral Arterial Disease 1990-2021 and Projections to 2050: 2021 Global Burden of Disease Study 2021
abstract: Background: The global and regional burden of lower-extremity peripheral artery disease (LEAD) and its trends have not been systematically studied. Utilising data from the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2021, this study analyses the global burden of disease and associated risk factors for LEAD from 1990 to 2021 and predicts its incidence trends to 2050. Method(s): LEAD-related data from different age groups worldwide were extracted from the GBD 2021 database, including the number of morbidities, mortality, disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), age-standardised rate (ASR), and 95% uncertainty interval (UI). The analysis assesses the burden of LEAD globally and across regions stratified by social demographic index (SDI), age, and sex. Bayesian age-period-cohort models (BAPC) were used to predict the future age-standardised incidence of LEAD. Finding(s): The global incidence, deaths, and DALYs for LEAD increased significantly between 1990 and 2021; however, age-standardised incidence rates (ASIR), age-standardised rates of deaths (ASMR), and age-standardised disability-adjusted life years (ASDR) showed an overall decline. In particular, the ASIR declined from 130.33/100,000 (95% [UI] 112.75,149.44) in 1990 to 115.44/100,000 (95% [UI] 100.04,132.72) in 2021, with the most pronounced decline occurring between 1990 and 2007. Regionally, the ASIR was highest in high SDI North America, whereas ASMR and DALYs were more pronounced in Eastern Europe. In addition, ASIR and SDI were positively correlated. Age-specific analyses revealed that ASMR increased with age, with ASIR peaking in individuals aged 75-79 years. Predictions from the BAPC model indicate a slight increase in ASIR for global LEAD over the next 29 years. High fasting glucose was the leading DALY risk factor in both sexes globally, followed by renal dysfunction, smoking, high SDI, and hypertension. Interpretation(s): The disease burden of LEAD increases progressively with age, and its prevalence is mainly influenced by SDI. Despite the increased incidence of LEAD in women, mortality and DALYs were substantially higher in men. The global burden of LEAD is projected to increase progressively by 2050, representing a major health concern. title_screening: Global Incidence, Prevalence, Deaths and Disease Burden of Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension:A 30-Year Overview and Projected Trends
abstract: Background: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a critical condition marked by elevated pulmonary artery pressure, leading to considerable morbidity and mortality, which poses a substantial burden on healthcare systems globally. This study seeks to clarify the epidemiological trends and burden of PAH across various demographics and regions, highlighting gaps in understanding its impact and risk factors. Method(s): We analyzed 31 years of Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2021 data on PAH, focusing on incidence, prevalence, mortality, disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), age-standardized rates (ASRs), and average annual percentage change (AAPC). Joinpoint regression analysis was employed to detect temporal changes and estimate annual percentage change (APC) of each trend segment.Measures were stratified by sex, age, and socio-demographic index (SDI).Finally,the Bayesian age-period-cohort (BAPC) model was used to predict the future disease burden in the next 20 years. Result(s): Our findings indicate that the global prevalence of PAH rose from 105,703 cases in 1990 to 191,808 cases in 2021, with age-standardized prevalence remaining stable. While PAH-related deaths rose from 14,842 to 22,021, age-standardized mortality rates declined, indicating better management strategies. Notably, males exhibited a more significant reduction in ASMR and ASDR compared to females. Regions with lower SDI showed higher age-standardized PAH rates, highlighting the need for focused public health efforts there. Projections suggest ASMR will keep declining until 2040, while the total number of PAH cases, especially in females, is expected to increase. Conclusion(s): This study highlights the critical need for continuous monitoring and customized interventions to improve patient outcomes and optimize the allocation of healthcare resources, given the dynamic challenges posed by the increasing burden of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). title_screening: Global Burden of Chronic Kidney Disease Attributable to High Body Mass Index from 1990 to 2021: Analysis of Data from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021
abstract:
Background: Obesity is an independent risk factor for chronic kidney disease (CKD), contributing significantly to its development. This study aimed to assess the global burden of CKD attributable to high BMI, analyze temporal trends from 1990 to 2021, and project future trends through 2035.
Methods: A population-based analysis using data from the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2021. Data from204 countries and territories across 21 GBD regions were included. Trends in age-standardized mortality rate (ASMR) and age-standardized DALYs rate (ASDR) were evaluated using percentage change (PC) and estimated annual percentage change (EAPC). Decomposition analysis identified key contributors to changes in mortality and Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs). Projections were generated to estimate future burden through 2035.
Findings: The global burden of high BMI-attributable CKD has risen significantly, with substantial geographic and gender-related heterogeneity, particularly in low-, low-middle-, and middle-SDI regions. In males, the burden has shifted to younger age groups. Between 1990 and 2021, the ASMR rose from 2.69 (95% UI: 1.37-4.14) to 5.06 (95% UI: 2.7-7.5) per 100,000, and the ASDR increased from 69.13 (95% UI: 35.06-106) to 122.08 (95% UI: 66.25-180.18) per 100,000. By 2035, projections indicate ASMR and ASDR will reach 5.81 (95% UI: 3.55-8.07) and 149.42 (95% UI: 99.45-199.39) per 100,000, respectively. Hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) were the leading contributors to CKD-related mortality with gender-based disparities. Hypertension affected more males (42.05%), while T2DM had a more impact on females (43.71%). Males also showed a younger age distribution for CKD-related mortality and DALY.
Interpretation: The rising global burden of CKD attributable to high BMI, with substantial geographic and gender disparities, highlights the urgent need for targeted prevention and intervention strategies. Regions with low SDI and younger male populations require prioritized efforts to mitigate this escalating health crisis.

title_screening: The Global, Regional, and National Burden of Parkinson's Disease in 204 Countries and Territories, 1990-2021: A Systematic Analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021
abstract: Background: Parkinson's disease (PD) represents a prevalent neurodegenerative condition that leads to significant disability and contributes to a growing public health challenge worldwide. However, a comprehensive report on progress from 1990 to 2021 is still lacking, especially regarding the risk factors associated with PD by gender and age. This study aims to examine the patterns of PD incidence, mortality rates, and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) across all age groups, along with the risk factors linked to PD-related fatalities, spanning the years from 1990 to 2021. Methods: We retrieved data on PD from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021. The burden of PD was assessed using incidence, deaths, and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs), with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (UIs). Analyses were conducted globally, regionally, and nationally for the period between 1990 and 2021, stratified by age, sex, and the Socio-demographic Index (SDI). Estimated annual percentage changes (EAPCs) were calculated to assess temporal trends. Only cases directly attributable to PD were included, and a comorbidity correction was applied to ensure accurate estimation of the burden. Findings: Globally, an estimated 13.35 million (95% UI, 12.67-14.08) individuals were living with PD in 2021, accounting for a 220% increase (95% UI, 210%-229%) in cases from 1990 to 2021. PD deaths increased from 148,068 (95% UI, 135,802-158,149) in 1990 to 388,194 (95% UI, 347,250-417,388) in 2021, while global disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) attributed to PD rose from 53.51 (95% UI, 49.54-57.56) to 94.68 (95% UI, 85.37-103.11) per 100,000 population during the same period. Age-standardized incidence rates increased from 7.82 (95% UI, 6.95-8.75) to 16.92 (95% UI, 15.16-18.82) per 100,000 population, and age-standardized mortality rates rose from 2.78 (95% UI, 2.55-2.97) to 4.91 (95% UI, 4.40-5.29) per 100,000 population. Among the five Socio-demographic Index (SDI) regions, the high SDI region reported the highest all-age PD-associated mortality rate in 2021, while East Asia showed the largest increase in incidence, with an estimated annual percentage change (EAPC) of 5.15 (95% CI, 5.09-5.21). The burden of PD was most pronounced in elder populations, with the 85-89 age group experiencing the highest incidence rate (417.62 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 296.68-571.56), mortality rate (427.65 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 350.74-473.70), and DALYs (4262.54 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 3721.44-4681.33). Among 204 countries, Germany recorded the highest national incidence of PD in 2021 (53 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 51-55), while Monaco had the highest mortality rate (20.41 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 15.54-25.48) and the highest DALY rate (333.13 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 267.52-396.18).Globally, smoking was a key risk factor for PD-associated mortality in 2021. Among different age groups, the proportion of deaths attributable to smoking ranged from -9.09% in individuals aged 50-54 years to -2.69% in those aged 95 years and elder. Interpretation: PD represents a significant and escalating global health challenge, driven by increasing incidence rates and an aging population. This growing burden highlights the urgent need for effective strategies in prevention, early diagnosis, and tailored management, particularly for elder males who are disproportionately affected. Addressing modifiable risk factors and advancing etiological research are crucial to mitigating the rising prevalence and optimizing resource allocation. Coordinated public health interventions and robust healthcare policies are essential to reduce the global impact of PD and improve outcomes for affected individuals. title_screening: A global spatial analysis of factors associated with case and mortality rates for coronavirus disease 2019 during the first year of the pandemic
abstract: Background: A increasing number of studies have revealed associations between country-level determinants and coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) outcomes. This ecological study was conducted to analyze country-level parameters related to COVID-19 infections and deaths during the first year of the pandemic. Methods: The examined predictors comprised demographics, economic factors, disease prevalence and healthcare system status, and the relevant data were obtained from public databases. The index dates were set to 15 July 2020 (Time 1) and 15 December 2020 (Time 2). The adjusted spatial autoregression models used a first-order queen contiguity spatial weight for the main analysis and a second-order queen contiguity spatial weight for a sensitivity analysis to examine the predictors associated with COVID-19 case and mortality rates. Results: Obesity was significantly and positively associated with COVID-19 case and mortality rates in both the main and sensitivity analyses. The sensitivity analysis revealed that a country's gross domestic product, population density, life expectancy and proportion of the population older than 65 y are positively associated with COVID-19 case and mortality rates. Conclusion: With the increasing global prevalence of obesity, the relationship between obesity and COVID-19 disease at the country level must be clarified and continually monitored.

title_screening: Characteristics of COVID-19 patients and risk factors of mortality in the early times of pandemic, Herat-Afghanistan
abstract: Objective: Coronaviruses are a large family of viruses that cause different types of diseases. This study aims to evaluate the risk factors for mortality based on comorbidity and sociodemographic characteristics among COVID-19 patients. Methods: This cross-sectional study conducted in Herat, Afghanistan, from February 24 to July 5, 2020, used data provided by the public health department, including sociodemographics, symptoms, comorbidities, hospitalization, contact history, and COVID-19 test type. The Chi-square test was used to observe differences between categorical variables. In bivariate analysis, all independent variables with a significant p-value were put into the model. Odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals were calculated, and a p-value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: The study analyzed 11,183 COVID-19 cases, with a 53.5% positivity rate. Recovery rates in the city and Herat province districts were 96.2% and 94.7%, respectively. Case-fatality rates varied with age, with 0.4% for those aged 1-29 and 33% for those aged 80-105. Mortality rates were highest for those with COPD and cancer, at 12.5% and 18.2%, respectively. In the logistic regression results, age, gender, and COPD were significant variables for COVID-19 mortality. Conclusion: By providing more health service facilities to people in risk groups, especially in rural areas, the mortality rate of COVID-19 and other diseases can be decreased.

title_screening: Disaster mortalities and the Sendai Framework target a: insights from Zimbabwe
abstract: In many parts of the world, human losses to disasters have been on the increase during the past three decades. This has slowed down the human development process. In an attempt to curb disaster impact, the world adopted an action-oriented Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (SFDRR) in 2015. Target A of the SFDRR seeks to substantially reduce disaster mortalities by 2030. This study contributes to the SFDRR by bringing in disaster-disaggregated mortality data to assess the progress of Zimbabwe's commitment in attaining Target A. The data came from the Zimbabwe National Statistics Agency, the Traffic Safety Council of Zimbabwe, the Department of Civil Protection and the EM-DAT database. To analyse the data, we conducted 3-year and 5-year moving averages for a period of thirty years to frame a holistic picture of the disaster mortalities in Zimbabwe. We also applied the methodology developed by the Open-Ended Intergovernmental Expert Working Group to determine the mortality rates for the overall and individual disaster type. Results clearly showed that Zimbabwe is making progress in reducing disaster mortalities despite a few spikes across its range of disasters. Major deaths were caused by drought, diarrhoea, malaria and tropical cyclones. Therefore, Zimbabwe needs to invest in drought monitoring and mitigation, cyclone forecasting and early warnings, and the surveillance and prevention of diarrhoeal diseases and malaria in order to substantially reduce the disaster mortality by the year 2030.

title_screening: Understanding risk factors of a new variant outburst through global analysis of Omicron transmissibility
abstract: The emergence of a new virus variant is generally recognized by its usually sudden and rapid spread (outburst) in a certain world region. Due to the near-exponential rate of initial expansion, the new strain may not be detected at its true geographical origin but in the area with the most favorable conditions leading to the fastest exponential growth. Therefore, it is crucial to understand better the factors that promote such outbursts, which we address in the example of analyzing global Omicron transmissibility during its global emergence/outburst in November 2021-February 2022. As predictors, we assemble a number of potentially relevant factors: vaccinations (both full and boosters), different measures of population mobility (provided by Google), estimated stringency of measures, the prevalence of chronic diseases, population age, the timing of the outburst, and several other socio-demographic variables. As a proxy for natural immunity (prevalence of prior infections in population), we use cumulative numbers of COVID-19 deaths. As a response variable (transmissibility measure), we use the estimated effective reproduction number (R<sub>e</sub>) averaged in the vicinity of the outburst maxima. To select significant predictors of R<sub>e</sub>, we use machine learning regressions that employ feature selection, including methods based on ensembles of decision trees (Random Forest and Gradient Boosting). We identify the young population, earlier infection onset, higher mobility, low natural immunity, and low booster prevalence as likely direct risk factors. Interestingly, we find that all these risk factors were significantly higher for Africa, though curiously somewhat lower in Southern African countries (where the outburst emerged) compared to other African countries. Therefore, while the risk factors related to the virus transmissibility clearly promote the outburst of a new virus variant, specific regions/countries where the outburst actually happens may be related to less evident factors, possibly random in nature.

title_screening: Mapping the global spatio-temporal dynamics of COVID-19 outbreak using cartograms during the first 150 days of the pandemic
abstract: The novel coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic is a public health emergency of international concern that caused disaster consequences all over the world. To mitigate and manage the pandemic, geographical information systems (GIS)-based spatial analysis has been used in a key role. To this aim, many GIS-based maps are produced by many national and international institutions. However, the produced maps are prepared by conventional methods and the features in these maps representing by their areal size. This paper proposes the diffusion-based cartograms for visualization of the COVID-19 outbreak. In the study, daily country-level data of the first 150 days of the COVID-19 outbreak were obtained from WHO, and the spread and spatial patterns of the epidemic were presented according to the number of confirmed cases and deaths. As a result of the study, it was observed that the cartogram is a powerful visualization tool and superior to the classical methods.

title_screening: Two years of Cameroon's resilient response to the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: In the last two years, Cameroon has faced five waves of COVID-19, with its fourth wave of the B.1.1.529 Omicron variant in December 2021 and subsequently hosted the African Cup of Nation of Football Men's competition that gathered thousands of people from across the world in January 2022 with no increase in the number of cases/deaths. A fifth wave of BA.4, and BA.5 Omicron variants was seen in August 2022. The country as claimed 123 785 cases, 121 633 recovered and 1960 death by 30th September 2022. Despite a low vaccination coverage of 8.7% the country has seen a limited impact of COVID-19 as compared to the international prediction. The response of Cameroon focused in limiting the spread of the SARS-CoV-2 in the population, reducing the morbidity and mortality due to COVID-19 and limiting the socio economic impact of the COVID-19 in Cameroon. The contextualized Cameroonian response was based on an important epidemiologic surveillance relying on mass testing strategy and adaptative measure that ensure the continuity of the of planned mass gathering activities including hosting the African Cup of Nations of Football in the COVID-19 context and the continuity of education. While the COVID-19 has shown some weakness in the health system it has been an opportunity to show its resilience and the opportunity for strengthening the health system including the implementation of a genomic surveillance platform. The lessons learnt from COVID-19 including the importance of coordination through the Public Health Emergency Operating Centre will help the country to address the future public health emergencies and move toward cholera elimination by 2030.

title_screening: Can 4C score predict mortality due to COVID-19 pneumonia in Syria? An observational study
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The aim of this study was to investigate the patients treated for COVID -19 in pandemic hospitals in northwestern Syria. METHODS: The study evaluated all patients hospitalized for COVID -19 by the pandemic emergency departments of hospitals in northwestern Syria between July 1, 2020 and December 01, 2020. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, and imaging characteristics, 4C mortality index scores treatments, and progressions of all patients hospitalized for COVID -19 were retrospectively reviewed. RESULTS: A total of 991 patients admitted to hospitals in northwestern Syria by pandemic emergency services for treatment and follow-up were included. 114 patients from Afrin Hospital, 251 from Al-Bab Hospital, 527 from Azez Vatan Hospital, and 99 from Jarablus Hospital were included in the study. When comparing the mortality and hospitalization rates of the patients according to the 4C Mortality Score, it was found that the patients with high-risk score in Azez and Jarabulus hospitals and those with very high-risk score in El Bab hospital had significantly higher mortality and hospitalization rates in the ICU (p<0.05). DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION: The data that can be obtained from studies evaluating the approach to the COVID -19 epidemic in this and similar regions are important for the development of health services in disadvantaged regions. We believe that our study will make an important contribution to the literature, as it is the first and only data reflecting hospitalized patients with COVID -19 in this region.

The same was noticed with the mortality rate, with 14.5% of total cases and 66.4% of them were older than 65. Conclusion, significance and impact of study: Our study indicated that age and gender are risk factors for contracting COVID-19.

title_screening: The second wave of COVID-19 disease in haemodialysis patients: an experience of a dialysis center from Pakistan
abstract: Objective: To evaluate the characteristics and outcomes of second wave of coronavirus disease-2019 in haemodialysis patients. Method: The retrospective, observational cohort study was conducted at The Kidney Center Post-Graduate-Training-Institute, Karachi, Pakistan and comprised data of patients regardless of gender who contracted coronavirus disease-2019 during the second wave from November 3, 2020, till February 12, 2021. Epidemiological, clinical, laboratory, and radiological characteristics and outcomes of the patients were reviewed. Data was analysed using SPSS 21. Results: Of 437 patients on haemodialysis, 46(10.5%) contracted coronavirus disease-2019; 29(63%) males and 17(37%) females. The overall median age was 61.5+or-13.02 years. Most patients developed mild disease 27(%). The most common symptom was fever 29(63%), and 6(13.1%) patients had patchy bilateral opacity on chest radiograph. Major complications were lymphocytopenia 29(63%), pneumonia 15(32.6%), thrombocytopenia 8(17.4%), and septic shock 5(10.9%). Overall, 15(32.6%) patients required hospitalisation, and 8(17.4%) required mechanical ventilation. There were 13(28.3%) deaths. Patients aged >60 years had 6.8 times more severe disease (p=0.023) and chances of death among them were 5.8 times higher (p=0.036) than in those aged <60 years. Conclusion: There was a high susceptibility of haemodialysis patients during the second wave of coronavirus disease compared to the general population. The most important determinants of death were advanced age, lower oxygen saturation and thrombocytopenia at presentation.

title_screening: Risk factors of COVID-19 critical outcomes in the Eastern Mediterranean Region: multicountry retrospective study
abstract: Background: The establishment of empirical evidence in the Eastern Mediterranean Region necessitates the implementation of wide-scale studies to describe the demographic, clinical features, and severity profile of patients with COVID-19. Background: This study aims to assess the patterns of COVID-19 severity and mortality in seven countries, and to determine the risk factors of COVID-19 severity and mortality. Methods: This multicountry study was based on a retrospective review of medical records of hospitalized patients confirmed to have COVID-19. This study includes data from Iraq, Pakistan, Sudan, Somalia, Morocco, Egypt, and Yemen. All demographic and clinical data were extracted from hospital records (paper files) by trained data collectors. Results: A total of 4141 patients were included in this study from seven countries. Comorbidities were reported by nearly half of the patients, with hypertension (n=1021, 24.7%) and diabetes (n=939, 22.7%) being the most common. Older age, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and heart diseases were significantly associated with COVID-19 severity and mortality. Ever smoking and renal diseases were significantly associated with severity but not mortality, while male gender, respiratory diseases, and malignancy were significantly associated with mortality but not severity. Conclusion: The study confirms the role of comorbidities and demographic features on the severity and mortality of COVID-19. Understanding the contributing factors ensures attentive care and informs clinical management of patients with poorer prognoses in the early stages of diseases.

title_screening: Conflict and child mortality in Mali: a synthetic control analysis
abstract: Indirect effects of conflict on mortality of vulnerable groups are as important, or more important, than the direct effects. However, data limitations and methodological challenges hinder the estimation of excess deaths produced by conflict, and few studies explore the mechanisms by which conflict harms civilian populations. We estimate the impact of the Malian conflict on child mortality over the period 2012-2018 using Demographic Health Survey data. We use birth histories to build time series of child mortality, and we employ novel synthetic control methods to show that the Malian conflict significantly increased child mortality in northern Mali. We conduct a difference-in-difference analysis of the impact of conflict on key determinants of maternal and child health and conclude that a reduction in access to safe sanitation and to child vaccinations in conflict areas was among the most likely causes of the increase in mortality. Northern Mali is today one of the poorest and most neglected areas of the world where humanitarian assistance is urgently needed.

abstract: Objective: This study aimed to describe the trends in mortality from eight vaccine-preventable diseases in Colombia in the last 40 years and their relationship with vaccination coverage. Study design It is a population-based descriptive study. Methods: The frequencies of deaths by decade, disease, sex, and the specific mortality rates by age group were calculated. Using a negative binomial regression model, the 10-year changes in mortality and their relationship with vaccination coverage were determined. Results: The number of deaths and the adjusted rates decreased since 1989 in all diseases (incidence rate ratio <1 when compared with the 1979-1988 decade). Vaccination coverage below 90% is associated with an increase in mortality from diphtheria, measles, mumps, neonatal tetanus, and pertussis. Conclusion: Historical changes in mortality support the benefits of vaccination, but new efforts are required to sustain the elimination of diseases.

abstract: Objectives. Type of health insurance was the most important factor, accounting for 20% and 59% of the relative and absolute inequalities, respectively. Conclusions. Health insurance appears to be the main contributor to those inequalities, posing challenges for the design of public health strategies.

abstract: Background: There is no data published related to measles outbreaks in Libya. The study aims to report a descriptive analysis of measles outbreaks that occurred in 2018. Methods: Retrospective data of measles outbreaks in 2018 were analysed to describe the characteristics of the outbreaks and their incidence in Libya. Data were categorised as confirmed measles cases, district distribution, deaths, age distribution, sex ratio, monthly trends, and measles vaccination status in the outbreaks. Also, the measles virus genotype was identified and compared with the reference strain. Results: A total of 934 confirmed measles cases were detected in seven outbreaks in different locations of the country in 2018. The biggest outbreak was found in Zliten (449 measles cases, 48.0%) followed by Benghazi (374 measles cases, 40.0%). The majority were below 15 years (811 measles cases, 87.0%). Children with measles who had completed two doses of vaccines were 18.0%, whilst 62.0% were unvaccinated. The genotype sequence was identified in three outbreaks being B3. Conclusion: A significant measles incidence was detected in many outbreaks mainly in the age group below 15 years. The immunity building programme must be evaluated to address the weakness of routine immunisation.

Severe disease and mortality were observed among infants and children with co-morbidities.

title_screening: COVID-19 in the 47 countries of the WHO African region: a modelling analysis of past trends and future patterns
abstract: Background: COVID-19 has affected the African region in many ways. We aimed to generate robust information on the transmission dynamics of COVID-19 in this region since the beginning of the pandemic and throughout 2022. Methods: For each of the 47 countries of the WHO African region, we consolidated COVID-19 data from reported infections and deaths (from WHO statistics); published literature on socioecological, biophysical, and public health interventions; and immunity status and variants of concern, to build a dynamic and comprehensive picture of COVID-19 burden. The model is consolidated through a partially observed Markov decision process, with a Fourier series to produce observed patterns over time based on the SEIRD (denoting susceptible, exposed, infected, recovered, and dead) modelling framework. The model was set up to run weekly, by country, from the date the first infection was reported in each country until Dec 31, 2021. New variants were introduced into the model based on sequenced data reported by countries. The models were then extrapolated until the end of 2022 and included three scenarios based on possible new variants with varying transmissibility, severity, or immunogenicity. Findings: Between Jan 1, 2020, and Dec 31, 2021, our model estimates the number of SARS-CoV-2 infections in the African region to be 505.6 million (95% CI 476.0-536.2), inferring that only 1.4% (one in 71) of SARS-CoV-2 infections in the region were reported. Deaths are estimated at 439 500 (95% CI 344 374-574 785), with 35.3% (one in three) of these reported as COVID-19-related deaths. Although the number of infections were similar between 2020 and 2021, 81% of the deaths were in 2021.52.3% (95% CI 43.5-95.2) of the region's population is estimated to have some SARS-CoV-2 immunity, given vaccination coverage of 14.7% as of Dec 31, 2021. By the end of 2022, we estimate that infections will remain high, at around 166.2 million (95% CI 157.5-174.9) infections, but deaths will substantially reduce to 22 563 (14 970-38 831). Interpretation: The African region is estimated to have had a similar number of COVID-19 infections to that of the rest of the world, but with fewer deaths. Our model suggests that the current approach to SARS-CoV-2 testing is missing most infections. These results are consistent with findings from representative seroprevalence studies. There is, therefore, a need for surveillance of hospitalisations, comorbidities, and the emergence of new variants of concern, and scale-up of representative seroprevalence studies, as core response strategies.

title_screening: Effect of sotrovimab on hospitalization or death among high-risk patients with mild to moderate COVID-19. A randomized clinical trial
abstract: Importance: Older patients and those with comorbidities who are infected with SARS-CoV-2 may be at increased risk of hospitalization and death. Sotrovimab is a neutralizing antibody for the treatment of high-risk patients to prevent COVID-19 progression. Background: To evaluate the efficacy and adverse events of sotrovimab in preventing progression of mild to moderate COVID-19 to severe disease. Design, Setting, and Participants: Randomized clinical trial including 1057 nonhospitalized patients with symptomatic, mild to moderate COVID-19 and at least 1 risk factor for progression conducted at 57 sites in Brazil, Canada, Peru, Spain, and the US from August 27, 2020, through March 11, 2021; follow-up data were collected through April 8, 2021. Interventions: Patients were randomized (1:1) to an intravenous infusion with 500 mg of sotrovimab (n = 528) or placebo (n = 529). Main Outcomes and Measures: The primary outcome was the proportion of patients with COVID-19 progression through day 29 (all-cause hospitalization lasting >24 hours for acute illness management or death); 5 secondary outcomes were tested in hierarchal order, including a composite of all-cause emergency department (ED) visit, hospitalization of any duration for acute illness management, or death through day 29 and progression to severe or critical respiratory COVID-19 requiring supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation. Results: Enrollment was stopped early for efficacy at the prespecified interim analysis. Among 1057 patients randomized (median age, 53 years [IQR, 42-62], 20% were >=65 years of age, and 65% Latinx), the median duration of follow-up was 103 days for sotrovimab and 102 days for placebo. All-cause hospitalization lasting longer than 24 hours or death was significantly reduced with sotrovimab (6/528 [1%]) vs placebo (30/529 [6%]) (adjusted relative risk [RR], 0.21 [95% CI, 0.09 to 0.50]; absolute difference, -4.53% [95% CI, -6.70% to -2.37%]; P < .001). Four of the 5 secondary outcomes were statistically significant in favor of sotrovimab, including reduced ED visit, hospitalization, or death (13/528 [2%] for sotrovimab vs 39/529 [7%] for placebo; adjusted RR, 0.34 [95% CI, 0.19 to 0.63]; absolute difference, -4.91% [95% CI, -7.50% to -2.32%]; P < .001) and progression to severe or critical respiratory COVID-19 (7/528 [1%] for sotrovimab vs 28/529 [5%] for placebo; adjusted RR, 0.26 [95% CI, 0.12 to 0.59]; absolute difference, -3.97% [95% CI, -6.11% to -1.82%]; P = .002). Adverse events were infrequent and similar between treatment groups (22% for sotrovimab vs 23% for placebo); the most common events were diarrhea with sotrovimab (n = 8; 2%) and COVID-19 pneumonia with placebo (n = 22; 4%). Conclusions and Relevance: Among nonhospitalized patients with mild to moderate COVID-19 and at risk of disease progression, a single intravenous dose of sotrovimab, compared with placebo, significantly reduced the risk of a composite end point of all-cause hospitalization or death through day 29. The findings support sotrovimab as a treatment option for nonhospitalized, high-risk patients with mild to moderate COVID-19, although efficacy against SARS-CoV-2 variants that have emerged since the study was completed is unknown.
